<h2 class="section">The hike</h2>
```

Drove up the N4 with three hours of David Goggins on the speakers explaining that I was, on the whole, soft. I parked at the base of Gleniff Horseshoe with my self image somewhat dented and my motivation correspondingly elevated.

Sligo is the county nobody talks about, which is criminal. Benbulbin is on every postcard, sure, but the rest of it goes underrated. Yeats is buried in Drumcliffe under it. He had taste.

The Gleniff Horseshoe is a loop walk that takes you up and around the back of the Benbulbin range, past the cliffs of Annacoona, past the cave where Diarmuid and Grainne supposedly hid out, and back round to the start. Eleven kilometres. Not technical. Just long, and very, very Irish.

The cliffs on the inside of the horseshoe go on for kilometres. They are stratified limestone laid down 320 million years ago when this was all a tropical sea. You stand on a bog at the base of them and it is genuinely, geologically humbling. Then you eat a banana.

The full moon came up behind Benbulbin while I was still on the ridge. The cliffs went pink and the moon was the size of a saucer. I am aware that the moon being the size of a saucer is the kind of thing you read in a sixth year English essay. It was, however, the size of a saucer.

Then I drove down to Mullaghmore as the light dropped. Classiebawn Castle was a black silhouette against a sky the colour of a fresh bruise, and I took a photo from the field across the road. It is one of the best photos I have ever taken. Sligo gave me that photo for free.

<h2 class="section">Reflections</h2>
```

Sligo is two and a half hours from Dublin, on a road that improves the further you get from Dublin. There is a metaphor in there.

Glencar Waterfall and Glencar Lough at sunrise: sit in the car park, drink a coffee, look at it. You will not regret it.

If a Sligo local tells you Mullaghmore has the heaviest big-wave surf in Europe, they are not exaggerating. I went in February. I watched. I did not surf. I left intact.
